<reason>B set the decisive frame early: "only" makes each of the three rights individually necessary, so CON needs just one to fall. B then defeated work-as-necessary via the reception-support substitution and, crucially, answered A's best pressure question with a principled functional line (appeal corrects error and admits no substitute; work protects against destitution, which support can secure). Family unity never escaped the median-claimant objection, and B's knowable-in-advance distinction blunted A's appeal-rights analogy. A's capture/reabsorption argument was genuinely clever but drifted to a different principle — enforceable protection of underlying interests — rather than the motion's three named rights, which B's closing arithmetic ("one was defended; two were substituted, relabeled, or surrendered") accurately exposed. A's refoulement-by-attrition chain was asserted, not shown. Both sides were disciplined and well-grounded; symmetric clipping evened out execution costs. B made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 A1: facing A's strongest pressure (why can't appeal be excused by "careful first decisions" if work can be excused by substitutes?), B drew a clean functional line — error-correction has no substitute, destitution does — then compounded it in B4.6 by showing A's own Canada answer ran on enforceable adjudication, leaving work and family as "scenery."</best_rebuttal>
